beats.say: Welcome to Advanced Models.
In this module, the model gets data with no labels, and has to discover the structure by itself.
Unsupervised learning gets no labels. The model has to find the groups itself.
Hard clustering, like K-means, puts each point in exactly one cluster. Ana is in group two, full stop.
Soft clustering, like a Gaussian mixture, gives a probability for every cluster: seventy percent group two, thirty percent group three.
Cara is borderline. The soft model shows the doubt; the hard model just picks group three.
Eight customers, plotted by two features, with no labels. We ask K-means for two clusters.
Start: pick two data points as the first centroids. These two crosses.
Assign: every point joins its nearest centroid. Only two points pick the lower cross; the other six pick the upper one.
Update: each centroid moves to the mean of its points.
Assign again. Two points on the left are now closer to the first centroid, so they switch.
Update again. Each centroid lands in the middle of its four points.
One more assign changes nothing. That's convergence. The sum of squared distances, S S E, fell from thirteen thousand six hundred to six hundred and eighty-seven point five.
In the course lab, you can step through this yourself.
You choose k yourself. The elbow method works out S S E for k equals one, two, three and so on.
beats.sql: SSE = sum of squared distances to each point's centroid

beats.say: One cluster leaves a huge S S E: almost eight thousand.
Two clusters cut it by seven thousand two hundred and fifty.
After that, extra clusters only shave off a couple of hundred each.
The curve bends sharply at two. That's the elbow, so k equals two.
Watch out: K-means can get stuck depending on where it starts, so run it several times. And it likes round clusters.

scenes.title: Other ways to cluster
rows: Merge or split into a tree

beats.say: K-means is one family. Here are five.
Centroid-based methods give each cluster a centre. Fast, for round clusters.
Density-based methods, like D B SCAN, find crowded areas. They handle odd shapes and label lonely points as noise.
Hierarchical methods build a tree of merges or splits, showing clusters at many levels.
Distribution-based methods, like a Gaussian mixture, give soft, oval-shaped clusters.
And fuzzy methods let a point belong partly to several overlapping groups.
Don't mix up K-means with K nearest neighbours. K N N is classification, and it needs labels.
Association rules find items bought together. Here are ten shopping baskets.
beats.note: Br = bread · Bu = butter · Mk = milk

beats.say: Bread is in five baskets.
Butter is in three, and all three also have bread.
Milk is in nine of the ten baskets. Almost everyone buys it.
Bread and milk together: four baskets.
Support: baskets with both, divided by all baskets. Three out of ten.
beats.sql: Support = baskets with X and Y ÷ all baskets

beats.say: Confidence: of the five bread baskets, three have butter. Point six.
beats.sql: Confidence = baskets with X and Y ÷ baskets with X

beats.say: Lift divides that by how common butter is anyway, point three. Lift two: bread really does make butter more likely.
beats.sql: Lift = Confidence ÷ (baskets with Y ÷ all baskets)

beats.say: Bread to milk looks better on confidence: point eight.
But milk is in nine baskets out of ten anyway. Lift is point eight nine, below one: no real link.
Lift above one is a positive link, one is no link, below one is negative. Try the rule calculator in the lab.

scenes.title: What does K-means do in the update step?
options: Moves each centroid to the mean of its assigned points
scenes.good: That's right. Update means recomputing each centroid as the average of its points. Assign gives each point to its nearest centroid.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Update means recomputing each centroid as the average of its points. Assign gives each point to its nearest centroid.

beats.say: Quick check.
What does K-means do in the update step?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 1.
You're done when:
you can explain that unsupervised models discover structure without labels,
you can run K-means: assign, update, repeat,
you can match cluster shapes to methods like D B SCAN and Gaussian mixtures,
and you can score a rule with support, confidence and lift.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 2.
A three D object casts a two D shadow. Hold it at the right angle, and the shadow still shows most of its shape. Dimensionality reduction looks for that best angle.

scenes.title: Why reduce dimensions?
rows: Hard to choose how many to keep

beats.say: Each feature is one measurement. A tiny sixty-four by sixty-four grey image already has four thousand and ninety-six of them.
With fewer features, training is faster.
The data is easier to plot and understand.
And models overfit less, because there's less room to find accidental patterns. That's the curse of dimensionality.
The price: some information is lost, and if you cut too far, accuracy drops.
Feature selection keeps some original features and drops the rest. Filter methods score each one on its own.
Missing value ratio: income is missing for sixty-five percent of people. Drop it.
Low variance: sensor I D has only one value, so it tells us nothing. Drop it.
High correlation: height in inches copies height in centimetres exactly. Keep one, drop the other.
beats.sql: drop one of a pair with correlation > 0.95

beats.say: Age and height in centimetres survive.
Wrapper methods try subsets with a model; embedded methods, like random forest importance, decide while training.
Feature extraction instead builds new features from the old ones, like P C A.
Eight points with two features. They're strongly related: when one goes up, so does the other.
P C A looks for the direction where the data spreads out most. That's this diagonal line: principal component one.
Principal component two sits at ninety degrees. Along it, the points barely spread at all.
So we keep P C one, and project every point onto it. Each point becomes one number.
Points on either side of the line land on the same spot. The only thing lost is each point's small distance from the line.
In the course lab, raise the correlation and watch nearly all the spread line up along P C one.

scenes.title: The same eight points, by the numbers

beats.say: Step one: standardise. Subtract the mean, fifty, and divide by the standard deviation, about twenty-two point five.
Step two: the covariance matrix. The two features move together with a score of point nine three.
Step three: eigenvectors and eigenvalues. P C one points along the diagonal, with eigenvalue one point nine three.
P C two is at ninety degrees, with eigenvalue just point zero seven.
Step four: keep the top component. One number now carries ninety-six point five percent of the variance of two.
With more features, how many components do we keep? Each one's share is its eigenvalue divided by the total.
beats.sql: explained variance of PCi = λi ÷ (λ1 + λ2 + … + λn)

beats.say: Four eigenvalues add up to six. P C one is four point two out of six: seventy percent.
P C two adds eighteen percent. Together, eighty-eight percent, with half the features.
A common rule is to reach about ninety to ninety-five percent. Here, adding P C three gets us to ninety-five.
P C A compresses image features, powers eigenfaces, and plots big datasets in two D.

scenes.title: Eigenvalues are 6, 3 and 1. What share does PC1 explain?
scenes.good: That's right. Six divided by six plus three plus one is point six, so sixty percent.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Six divided by six plus three plus one is point six, so sixty percent.

beats.say: Quick check.
Eigenvalues are six, three and one. What share does P C one explain?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 2.
You're done when:
you can say why too many features slow training and cause overfitting,
you can tell selection, which keeps original features, from extraction, which builds new ones,
you can follow P C A: standardise, covariance, eigenvectors, keep the top k,
and you can choose k with cumulative explained variance.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 3.
Classification gives one label for a whole image. Object detection finds every object, draws a box around each, and labels it.
YOLO, short for You Only Look Once, does it all in a single pass through one network, fast enough for real-time video.

scenes.title: One pass, from pixels to predictions

beats.say: Older detectors worked in two stages: propose regions, then classify each one. YOLO uses one network, once.
The image is resized to four hundred and forty-eight pixels square.
A backbone of twenty-four convolutional layers and four pooling layers extracts features.
Two fully connected layers turn those features into predictions.
The last layer outputs one thousand four hundred and seventy numbers, reshaped into a seven by seven by thirty cube.
During training, the loss adds up three squared errors: box position, confidence, and class.
YOLO splits the image into an S by S grid. With S equals seven, each cell is sixty-four pixels.
The cell that holds an object's centre is responsible for detecting it. The dog's centre is at one fifty, three hundred.
One fifty divided by sixty-four is two point three, so the third column. Three hundred gives the fifth row.
The person's centre lands in the seventh column, second row. Only that cell predicts the person.
In the course lab, you can move objects around the grid and see which cell lights up.
Here's what one cell outputs in the original YOLO.
Box one: x and y, the box centre inside the cell, then width, height and a confidence score. Five numbers.
For the dog's cell, x is point three four and y is point six nine of the way across the cell.
B equals two, so a second box adds five more.
Then C equals twenty class probabilities: person, car, dog, and so on.
Thirty numbers per cell, times forty-nine cells, is one thousand four hundred and seventy.
We judge a predicted box against the true box with intersection over union, I o U. All boxes are ten by ten.
beats.sql: IoU = area of overlap ÷ area of union

beats.say: A perfect match overlaps completely: one hundred over one hundred. I o U is one.
Shift it five to the right: the overlap is fifty. The union is a hundred plus a hundred minus fifty. I o U is point three three.
A detection usually counts as correct at point five or more. Shifted by two passes; shifted by five fails.
Box confidence multiplies the chance there's an object by the I o U. Point nine times point six seven is point six.
The dog score multiplies that by the dog probability, point eight: point four eight. Drag a box in the lab's I o U tab to see it change.
beats.sql: class score = Pr(dog | object) × box confidence = 0.8 × 0.60 = 0.48

beats.say: Duplicates are common. Here are five boxes around two dogs.
First, drop boxes below the confidence threshold, point three. Box five goes.
Keep the most confident box: box one, at point nine two.
Box two overlaps box one with I o U point seven two, above point five. It's a duplicate, so it's deleted.
beats.sql: 3. delete boxes with IoU > 0.5 against it

beats.say: Repeat with the next best: box three. It barely overlaps box one, so it's a second dog. Keep it.
Box four overlaps box three at point six five. Deleted.
Two clean boxes are left, one per dog. Later YOLOs added anchors and multiple scales, but kept the one fast pass.

scenes.title: Which grid cell is responsible for an object?
options: The cell containing the object's centre
scenes.good: That's right. Only the cell holding the object's centre predicts it, which avoids double counting.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Only the cell holding the object's centre predicts it, which avoids double counting.

beats.say: Quick check.
Which grid cell is responsible for an object?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 3.
You're done when:
you can explain detection as what plus where, in one network pass,
you can work out the output size, S times S times five B plus C,
you can compute I o U for two boxes,
and you can explain how non-maximum suppression removes duplicates.

Welcome to Module 4.
Transformers were invented for text. The Vision Transformer, or V I T, makes an image look like a sentence of tokens.
A convolutional network slides small filters across the image. The first layers find edges.
Stack layers, with pooling shrinking the image, and edges become textures, then parts, then whole objects.
The built-in idea is locality. The downside: far-apart regions only meet after many layers.
V I T cuts the image into equal squares called patches. Take a two twenty-four pixel image and sixteen pixel patches.
Two twenty-four divided by sixteen is fourteen patches per side.
Fourteen times fourteen is one hundred and ninety-six patches.
Each patch holds sixteen by sixteen pixels, times three colours: seven hundred and sixty-eight values.
Each patch is flattened and multiplied by a learned matrix: an embedding of size D.
Attention ignores order, so a positional embedding says where each patch came from.
And an extra C L S token goes at the front. It gathers information from every patch for the classifier. One hundred and ninety-seven tokens.
Each token makes a query, what am I looking for, a key, what do I contain, and a value, what will I pass on. Follow the dog head patch.
Its query is matched against every key. The dog body scores high, the sky low.
Scores are divided by the square root of d, here two, so they don't get too large.
Softmax turns the scores into weights that add up to one. The head keeps point four five for itself, and borrows point three from the body.
The sky only gets point zero eight.
The output is the weighted mix of the values: about point six nine. Mostly dog.
Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel. Click a patch in the lab to see its weights.
The tokens enter an encoder block.
LayerNorm rescales each token to a steady range, which keeps training stable.
Then multi-head self-attention mixes information between tokens.
A residual connection adds the block's input back to its output, so information and gradients can skip ahead.
Then another LayerNorm, and a feed-forward network with GELU, on each token separately.
And a second residual connection.
V I T Base stacks twelve of these. At the end, the C L S token goes through a small M L P head that outputs class probabilities.
A C N N looks at small local windows. V I T looks at every patch at once. Swin looks at local windows that shift each layer.
V I T has few built-in assumptions, so it learns from data, and needs lots of it, or pre-training.
And V I T's cost grows with N squared, because every pair of tokens is compared.
A two twenty-four image has one hundred and ninety-six patches. V I T compares every pair: thirty-eight thousand four hundred and sixteen.
Swin only attends inside windows of seven by seven patches. Four windows, forty-nine squared pairs each: nine thousand six hundred and four.
Double the image side. V I T's pairs jump sixteen times, to over six hundred thousand.
Swin's grow only four times, in step with the image. It also merges patches deeper down, building a pyramid like a C N N.
Tick Swin-style local windows in the lab to compare the counts yourself.

scenes.title: A 256 × 256 image with 32 × 32 patches gives how many patch tokens?
scenes.good: That's right. Two fifty-six divided by thirty-two is eight, and eight times eight is sixty-four.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Two fifty-six divided by thirty-two is eight, and eight times eight is sixty-four.

beats.say: Quick check.
A two fifty-six by two fifty-six image, cut into thirty-two by thirty-two patches. How many patch tokens?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 4.
You're done when:
you can turn an image into a sequence of patch tokens,
you can explain positional embeddings and the C L S token,
you can describe attention with queries, keys and values,
and you can compare C N Ns, V I T and Swin.

Welcome to Module 5.
Most models so far were discriminative: given an image, predict a label. A generative model learns what the data itself looks like, so it can create new examples.
Uses include image synthesis, extra training data, filling in missing parts of images, and anomaly detection.
A generative adversarial network has two networks that compete.
The generator takes random noise and turns it into a fake sample. It's the art forger.
The discriminator is the detective. It looks at a sample, real or fake.
And outputs the probability that it's real.
Each caught fake makes the forger better. Each fake that slips through makes the detective sharper.
In the end the fakes are so good that D can only guess: about point five.
Step one trains the discriminator. G makes a batch of fakes from noise.
D sees real images, with target label one.
And the fakes, with target label zero.
D's loss measures how wrong its probabilities were, and only D is updated.
Step two trains the generator. G makes new fakes, and D scores them.
G's loss compares those scores to the label G wants: one, real.
The error flows back through D into G, and only G is updated.
Repeat for many rounds. If D wins too easily, G learns nothing, and G may collapse to a few outputs. The lab trains a tiny GAN live.
An autoencoder squeezes an input through a small middle layer, then rebuilds it.
A plain autoencoder maps each input to one exact point, which leaves gaps. Decode a random point and you may get nonsense.
A variational autoencoder's encoder outputs a mean, mu, and a spread, sigma. A small cloud, not a point.
We take random noise, epsilon, from a standard normal.
And build the code: z equals mu plus sigma times epsilon.
The decoder rebuilds the input from z.
Say the encoder outputs mu equals one point five and sigma equals point four.
With zero noise, z is just the mean: one point five.
Noise of point five nudges it up to one point seven.
Minus one pulls it down to one point one. Each sample lands somewhere in the cloud.
The randomness lives only in epsilon. Mu and sigma are plain multiplications, so we can still backpropagate through them.
The V A E loss adds two parts.
beats.sql: VAE loss = reconstruction loss + KL divergence

beats.say: Reconstruction loss: how different the output is from the input. It keeps outputs faithful.
K L divergence: how far each encoded cloud is from a standard normal. It keeps the latent space smooth and filled in.
Because it's smooth, nearby codes decode to similar outputs, and walking between two codes morphs one output into another.
To make something new, sample z from a standard normal and run the decoder. Try it in the V A E tab of the lab.
A GAN trains two networks that compete. A V A E is one encoder and decoder with a loss.
GAN outputs are very sharp. V A E outputs are often a little blurry.
But V A Es train stably, and their smooth latent space is easy to explore.
Today's leading image generators are diffusion models. They start from pure noise and remove it step by step.

scenes.title: What does the KL term in the VAE loss do?
options: Keeps the latent space close to N(0, 1) so it is smooth
scenes.good: That's right. It stops the encoder from scattering codes far apart, leaving no gaps.
scenes.bad: Not quite. It stops the encoder from scattering codes far apart, leaving no gaps.

beats.say: Quick check.
What does the K L term in the V A E loss do?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 5.
You're done when:
you can explain the generator versus discriminator game,
you can walk through one round of GAN training,
you can describe the encoder, latent space and decoder of a V A E,
and you can explain the reparameterisation trick and the two parts of the loss.

Welcome to the last module.
A large language model is a very large transformer trained on huge amounts of text. At its core it does one thing: predict the next token.
Repeat that over and over, and you get paragraphs, code and conversations.
Text is split into tokens: words, pieces of words, or characters. Unbelievable might become un, believ, able.
Here our sentence is ten tokens.
Each token becomes an embedding, a vector of numbers. Words used in similar ways get similar vectors.
Self-attention lets each token look at the others. When the model reads it, attention links it to ball.
In a text generator, each token only looks at earlier tokens. Was and light come later, so it can't see them.
Here is one row of attention weights: how much the token it borrows from each earlier token.
Its query is matched against every key, and softmax turns the scores into weights that add up to one.
Ball gets half of all the attention. So its new meaning is mostly about the ball.
Robot is the runner-up, at point one eight.
The little words, like the and up, get almost nothing.
The model gives a raw score, a logit, to every token in the vocabulary. Here are five candidates after it was.
beats.sql: The robot picked up the ball because it was …

beats.say: Softmax turns the logits into probabilities. At temperature one, light gets fifty-six percent.
Low temperature, point two, divides by a small number and sharpens everything. Light gets ninety-nine percent: focused and repeatable.
High temperature, one point five, flattens the odds. Red rises from four to eight percent: more variety, more risk.
Top k only allows the k most likely tokens. With k equals three, light, heavy and round share the probability: sixty-three, twenty-three and fourteen percent.
Try both settings in the sampling tab of the lab.
Pre-training is self-supervised. The text supplies its own answers, because the label is simply the next word.
The model predicts, compares with the real next token, and adjusts its weights by gradient descent, billions of times.
Supervised fine-tuning trains on example prompts paired with good answers. Instruction tuning adds many tasks written as instructions.
In R L H F, people rank answers, a reward model learns their preferences, and the model is tuned to score well.
Reasoning models go further, with reinforcement learning that rewards breaking hard problems into steps.
The context window is the most the model can read at once: your prompt plus its answer. Anything outside it is not seen.
Retrieval-augmented generation, R A G, starts by searching a document collection with the question.
The most relevant passages are placed into the context window.
Along with the question itself, and clear instructions.
The model reads it all, so it can answer from up-to-date or private information without retraining.
But L L Ms can state wrong things confidently. That's hallucination. Check important claims.
Generative A I starts from a foundation model trained on broad data, like an L L M.
Next, tune it for a specific job, with fine-tuning, R L H F, or just good prompts and R A G.
Then generate, evaluate the outputs for accuracy and quality, and keep refining.
Multimodal models also turn image patches into tokens, exactly as V I T does. That's how a model can describe a video frame.

scenes.title: You want the same, focused answer every time. Temperature should be…
scenes.good: That's right. Low temperature sharpens the probabilities towards the top token.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Low temperature sharpens the probabilities towards the top token.

beats.say: Quick check.
You want the same, focused answer every time. What should the temperature be?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 6.
You're done when:
you can trace text from tokens to a next-token prediction,
you can explain self-attention in a sentence,
you can describe pre-training, fine-tuning and R L H F,
